label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017

# Cold Room, Warm Beer, and One Very Wet Trolley: A Cup Day Post-Mortem for Jonno

Jonno.

Mate. You've asked me four times now what happened with the coolroom on Cup Day. Four. I've started drafting replies and deleted them because typing the whole thing out on a phone while standing in a walk-in with gloves on is a nightmare, so here it is in one hit. Read it, don't read it, I don't care. Mostly you, probably, and my mum.

First up: yes, it was as bad as the story made it look. Worse, honestly. And no, you would not have handled it. London has made you soft. You'd of cried. You'd of stood in the laneway in your little jacket with a keep cup and cried.

## The discovery

So the compressor on the main coolroom died overnight, Monday the 2nd into Tuesday the 3rd. Nobody heard it. Coolrooms don't bang or scream, they just quietly stop being cold and get on with their day.

I found out at 6.40am on Cup Day. Walked in, and there's that smell — that specific smell where cold stuff has been sitting at the wrong temperature for a few hours and has started having opinions. Thermometer said 11 degrees. Eleven. On a day where we had 140 covers booked on a set three-course menu.

I rang Wally from Coldline. Wally is a good man and Wally was already booked solid, and the part had to come from Sydney, so the earliest he could get to us was Wednesday. Wednesday. Cool. Cool cool cool. Great.

Then I rang Phil. You know what Phil said? "Just make it work mate." That's it. That's the whole contingency plan. "Just make it work." I've thought about it a lot since and I'm fairly sure it's not a plan. It's a mood.

## The great relocation

Raff was off, so it was on me. Happy Cup Day to me.

Benny and I spent the next hour and a half doing the world's least glamorous removalist job. Everything out of the big coolroom and jammed into whatever cold space existed — the two undercounters, the bar fridge, and half of Marta's walk-in next door because Marta is a saint who took one look at my face and said "yeah, alright."

You should've seen the undercounters. If you opened one of those doors on Cup Day you'd have been hit in the shins by a wall of duck legs and dairy. It was like cold storage Jenga. Nothing was where it lived. For the rest of service every single thing took four times as long because nothing was where it lived.

Lost about $1800 of stock. Mostly dairy and the duck legs. Don't say anything to Phil about the number, he's already done his own maths and his maths always lands on "and whose fault is that."

## The trolley incident

Now. The beef shin.

30kg of it, down the laneway from the store room, in the rain, on a milk crate trolley. One wheel decided Cup Day was the day it retired and fell off about eight metres in. So it's me and Benny, in the rain, going full tug-of-war with a trolley that's now dragging on one corner and fighting us the whole way, both of us soaked, both of us laughing in that way where you're either laughing or you're going to sit down on the wet bitumen and give up on your life.

A woman on table 9 watched this out the window and later asked me, very sincerely, if the beef was "free range from the laneway."

I said yes. I said yes and I walked away. I regret nothing.

## Kev

Dishy Kev, absolute legend, gets sent to the servo to buy ice. Comes back with 14 bags in the boot of his Corolla. The servo guy apparently asked him if he was having a party.

Kev said "yeah."

Kev then filled the big old esky out the back with it, which became our emergency cold anything zone for the day. Genuinely, if Kev doesn't do that, we don't get through it. Kev, if you're reading this, which you won't, you're a king.

## Service

Here's the bit that makes no sense.

12.15pm, we 86 the panna cotta. Just gone. Can't hold it, can't serve it warm, no. So dessert became "affogato with whatever" — whatever's in the freezer, whatever survived, whatever I could wring out of the situation. And people loved it MORE. More! Someone went to the trouble of telling the front of house it was the best dessert they'd had all year. The best. All year.

I could've put a raspberry on a brick and they'd have asked for the recipe, that's what kind of day it was.

And then, honestly — it was the best service we've done all year. I mean that. 140 covers, everything half a metre from where it should be, half the crew running on coffee and spite, and everyone just locked in. FOH were firing. Kitchen was calm. Nobody had time to be precious about anything because there was no time. The whole thing just went.

Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite. That's the whole business model. You can dress it up with seasonal menus and natural wine but it's bar fridges and spite at the bottom of it.

## Housekeeping

- Marta got paid back in croissant credit. I owe her about three weeks of staff meal now and honestly I've accepted that as a permanent part of my life.
- My sweep horse was called Ice Cold Lad and he came second last. Second last. On that day. The universe is at best indifferent and at worst directly taking the piss out of me.
- I filled out the incident report. There is no incident report. I made a form. It has one line on it.

So yeah. That's what happened. Coolroom's fine now, Wally came Wednesday, part and all.

And Jonno — mate. You would've had a wonderful time. You'd of loved it. You'd of been at that servo buying 14 bags of ice with Kev and thinking it was the best day of your life. That's the bit that kills me about you being over there. Nobody's falling off a trolley in the rain in London, mate. Nobody's got a Marta. You're paying nineteen pounds for a pint and being polite about it.

Come home ya flog. There's a spot on the trolley with your name on it.

— [the name goes here]
